title: The Valley We Should Have Left
content:
The storm arrived before sunrise.

By the time Daniel opened his eyes, the small mountain shelter was trembling beneath the force of the wind. Rain struck the wooden walls so violently that it sounded like handfuls of stones being thrown against them.

He sat up and looked toward the opposite bed.

— Are you awake?

Maya was already standing beside the window.

— I've been awake for an hour.

Daniel pulled on his jacket.

— How bad is it?

She turned around.

— Bad enough that we shouldn't be here.

He walked toward the window.

Outside, the valley had disappeared behind a curtain of rain. The trail they had followed the previous afternoon was now hidden beneath streams of muddy water.

Their original plan had been simple: cross the valley, reach an abandoned mining station, and return to the village before nightfall.

Instead, they had spent the night in an old shelter after the weather deteriorated unexpectedly.

Daniel studied the landscape.

— The forecast said the storm would pass by noon.

Maya shook her head.

— I wish we'd checked the mountain report instead of trusting the general forecast.

He sighed.

— Me too.

Neither of them said anything for a moment.

They both knew that the mistake had been theirs.

They had ignored the advice of the local guide, who had warned them that weather conditions could change rapidly at that altitude.

At the time, they had laughed.

Now, the valley looked entirely different.

— We should wait — Maya said.

— Until when?

— Until the rain gets lighter.

Daniel looked at the trail.

— And if it doesn't?

Maya didn't answer.

By late morning, the rain had become even heavier.

Their food supplies were running low, and the shelter offered little protection from the cold.

Finally, Daniel picked up his backpack.

— We have to move.

Maya stared at him.

— Are you sure?

— No.

— That's reassuring.

— If we stay here overnight, we might run out of food.

She hesitated.

— I wish we hadn't come this way.

Daniel looked at her.

— You don't mean that.

— I do.

— No, you don't.

She gave him an irritated look.

— You always do that.

— Do what?

— Pretend everything will work out.

Daniel smiled weakly.

— It usually does.

— That's not a strategy.

He knew she was right.

They left the shelter shortly after noon.

The trail was difficult to follow. Several sections had disappeared beneath mud and fallen branches. They moved slowly, testing every step before placing their weight on the ground.

After an hour, they reached a fork.

One path descended toward the river.

The other climbed sharply toward the old mining station.

Daniel checked the map.

— The station is this way.

Maya looked toward the river.

— The lower path might be safer.

— It could also be flooded.

— The upper path looks unstable.

Daniel studied both routes.

— We need to decide.

Maya closed her eyes briefly.

— I wish we'd brought a satellite phone.

— So do I.

They chose the upper path.

Twenty minutes later, they heard a deep rumbling sound.

Daniel stopped.

— Did you hear that?

Maya nodded.

The ground shook beneath their feet.

Then part of the trail collapsed several meters ahead of them.

They stood frozen.

— We can't go back that way — Maya whispered.

Daniel looked behind them.

Another section of the trail had already begun to crumble.

— We have to keep moving.

They climbed.

The mining station appeared shortly before sunset.

It was little more than a stone building half buried beneath vegetation, but it offered protection from the storm.

Inside, they found an old table, several rusted tools, and a wooden cabinet.

Maya dropped her backpack.

— We're lucky.

Daniel looked at her.

— You don't believe that.

She smiled.

— Not really.

He walked toward the cabinet.

Inside was a collection of old maps.

One of them showed the entire valley.

Daniel spread it across the table.

There was another route leading out of the valley.

A narrow trail followed the mountainside and eventually connected with an old road.

— This could work.

Maya leaned over the map.

— Could?

— Should.

She pointed to a small symbol.

— What's that?

Daniel examined it.

— An emergency station.

— So there might be radio equipment.

— Exactly.

Maya smiled.

— Let's hope it still works.

They left before sunrise.

The storm had weakened, but the mountains remained dangerous.

After several hours of climbing, they reached the emergency station.

The door was unlocked.

Inside, they found an old radio.

Daniel turned it on.

Nothing happened.

He checked the cables.

— The battery is dead.

Maya sat down.

— Of course it is.

Daniel looked at the equipment.

— There might be another battery.

They searched the room.

Nothing.

Then Maya noticed a metal box beneath the desk.

Inside was a portable emergency beacon.

Daniel held it up.

— This might still work.

They activated it.

A faint light appeared.

Then another.

Finally, the device began transmitting.

Maya stared at him.

— Do you think someone will receive it?

— They should.

She smiled.

— I wish I could be certain.

Daniel sat beside her.

— So do I.

For the first time since they had entered the valley, neither of them tried to pretend they knew what would happen next.

They simply waited.

Three hours later, they heard a helicopter.

Maya looked toward the sky.

— Daniel.

He stood immediately.

The helicopter appeared between the mountains.

They waved frantically.

Within minutes, the rescue team had located them.

As they were being lifted from the valley, Maya looked down at the trail they had followed.

— If we'd listened to the guide, none of this would have happened.

Daniel smiled.

— That's true.

— If we'd checked the mountain report, we'd have stayed in the village.

— Also true.

— If we'd brought the satellite phone...

— We wouldn't have spent half a day looking for that emergency beacon.

Maya laughed.

Then her expression became serious.

— I wish we'd been more careful.

Daniel looked at her.

— Me too.

The helicopter rose higher.

The valley gradually disappeared beneath the clouds.

For several minutes, they remained silent.

Then Maya leaned toward him.

— Would you do it again?

Daniel thought about the storm, the collapsing trail, the cold, and the fear.

Then he smiled.

— Not exactly the same way.

— That's not what I asked.

He looked out of the window.

— Yes.

Maya shook her head.

— You're impossible.

— Probably.

She smiled.

— Next time, we're hiring a guide.

Daniel laughed.

— Definitely.

As the helicopter carried them away from the mountains, Daniel realized that regret was not always about wishing the past had never happened.

Sometimes, it was simply understanding what you should have done differently.

They could not change the decisions that had brought them into the valley.

They could, however, make sure those decisions did not become the ones that defined them.

And if they ever returned to those mountains, they would know better.

They would prepare differently.

They would listen.

And, most importantly, they would never again mistake confidence for certainty.
